title: Alternatives to Atomisation 2025 misation.pdf
author: Colin Foster
source: Mathematics Teaching 295, Association of Teachers of Mathematics (atm.org.uk), March
summary: Colin Foster challenges the assumption that breaking mathematical processes into small, sequential steps -- atomisation -- is the only viable way to manage working memory demands for novice learners. Using the example of adding fractions with unlike denominators, he argues that while atomisation can work, it produces 'arbitrary knowledge': lists of steps that are genuinely hard for both students and teachers to retain, requiring constant retrieval practice to avoid what he calls a 'spinning plates' problem, where the number of processes a student must keep active grows unmanageably as they learn more topics. His proposed alternative builds understanding through connections rather than isolated steps, using a number-line/fraction-wall diagram that lets students discover patterns (equivalent fractions in columns, families of denominators in rows) through guided discussion before ever writing a formal calculation. Foster walks through a full lesson sequence built on this diagram, arguing that because the knowledge is built through connections rather than an arbitrary sequence of steps, more mathematics learned this way makes the subject easier over time rather than harder, since students accumulate connections rather than an ever-growing list of separately memorized procedures.
points: Foster's central critique of atomisation is durability, not initial effectiveness: even competent teachers struggle to remember the exact sequence of steps they taught a few topics later, which suggests experts don't actually store the process as an ordered list of steps themselves.

His 'spinning plates' metaphor captures a scaling problem unique to atomisation: each atomised process requires ongoing retrieval practice to stay accessible, so the more processes a student learns this way, the more retrieval-practice time is consumed just maintaining prior learning.

The number-line/fraction-wall diagram operationalizes his alternative: rather than teaching add-fractions as an ordered step list, students discover the connections (equivalent fractions, common denominators) through structured 'what do you notice' discussion before any procedure is formalized.

Foster's claim that connected learning gets easier as you learn more (versus atomised learning, which gets harder as more processes accumulate) directly inverts the usual argument for atomisation as the more manageable approach for novices.
quotes: Breaking down mathematical processes for learners into sequences of small steps—atomising them—is often presented to teachers as a necessity. Anyone who questions this is likely to be accused of suffering from the 'curse of knowledge'.
I find that even teachers who themselves are perfectly competent at adding fractions struggle to remember a few topics later exactly what steps they taught to their class.
If these details are not to be forgotten, constant opportunities for retrieval practice will be needed, which becomes an increasing problem as more processes are learned.
I think of this as being like spinning plates—unless you return sufficiently often to each plate, it will come crashing down.
Alternatively, with a more connected approach to learning, the more mathematics you learn the easier the subject gets.
Many learners who succeed in mathematics say that one reason that they like it is that they do not have to remember much.
